newsitem.title: EL SALVADOR: Salvador president attacks textile boycott campaign.
newsitem.headline: Salvador president attacks textile boycott campaign.

text.p: El Salvador President Armando Calderon Sol on Wednesday denounced a U.S.-based campaign on the Internet urging consumers to boycott Salvadoran-made textiles, alleging use of sweatshop labor.
"I can do no less than consider them traitors, inhuman, for attacking the people and the Salvadoran family," Calderon told reporters.
Last October, a U.S. Labor Department special commission paid a visit to El Salvador in response to controversy over the country's so-called sweatshops, but ruled there were no widespread abuses.
The boycott campaign is being run by the Committee In Solidarity with the People of El Salvador (CISPES), an old nemesis of Calderon's ruling party, the National Republican Alliance (ARENA).

In the 1980s, CISPES, a U.S.-based leftist group, gained fame as one of the more outspoken critics of U.S. policy in El Salvador, when former President Ronald Reagan poured billions of dollars into this tiny Central American country to aid the government in its fight against Marxist guerrillas.
ARENA lawmakers accused the left-wing group of being "an appendix" of the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front (FMLN), the former guerrilla army that is now a legal political party.
The CISPES Web site "Sweat Gear Catalogue" accuses Salvadoran textile factories of unlawful firings, hiring minors and regularly closing shop without paying workers.
CISPES takes particular aim at Taiwanese- and Korean-owned textile factories in El Salvador's industrial free zone.
Hard copies of the "catalogue" have been distributed in U.S. discount and department stores like K Mart and J.C. Penney, a spokesman for the Salvadoran Association of Industry said.
"With this (campaign) they are taking bread off the table and taking away salaries and jobs from thousands of Salvadorans," Calderon said.
But FMLN Congressman Gerson Martinez rejected Calderon's complaints and pointed out that some textile factories had committed "flagrant violations".
"The ARENA government tolerates the violations," Martinez told reporters. "It looks like the so-called economic freedom is more like slavery for the labor sector."
